items.name: Kentucky Camp
items.description:
Historic camp with a small museum, H20, pit toilets. A nice place to take a break. Also possible to reserve the one very rustic cabin, great place to spend the night. Make reservations early, as it's often booked. | Kentucky Camp was built in 1904 as the headquarters of the Santa Rita Water and Mining Company, whose investors hoped to collect water from the Santa Rita Mountains for hydraulic gold mining. The venture was abandoned following the mysterious death of the chief engineer the following year. The property became a working cattle ranch for the next 50 years, before being sold to a mining conglomerate. The Coronado National Forest acquired the site in 1989; since then, the Forest and volunteers have been working together to preserve the site. Kentucky Camp (and associated features related to the development of the water system and mining in the area) is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

A unique feature of this site is its collection of five century-old adobe buildings. The ten room headquarters building is one of the largest surviving adobe buildings of its era. A three room adobe building is available for overnight rental. Go to the Forest Service "Cabins and Camping" web page for additional details on renting this building. (http://kentuckycamp.org/) Water tap.

items.name: San Rafael State Natural Area
items.description:
Starting in the counterclockwise direction, expansive views of the San Rafael State Natural Area welcome riders at the top of the first climb from Patagonia. The San Rafael State Natural Area is a unique area with rolling hills, native grasses, and oak and cottonwood trees. This beautiful valley serves as the headwaters of the Santa Cruz River, which flows into Mexico then turns north back into the United States and eventually joins the Gila River. While this valley is largely private land and used for cattle grazing, much of the valley is protected by conservation easements to ensure that the sustainable grazing practices that have preserved this valley continue (https://www.audubon.org/important-bird-areas/san-rafael-grasslands). 

The riparian areas and native grass prairie in the San Rafael State Natural Area are home to many species of plants and animals including; the endangered plant, Huachuca Water Umbel, the state-protected Sonoran Tiger Salamander, as well as mule deer, javalina, antelope, bobcats, cougar, coyote and many birds unique to the prairie. (https://azstateparks.com/san-rafael/about-the-ranch/about). As some of the last remaining un-fragmented prairie grassland habitat left in the American Southwest, this area is of vital importance for grassland bird species. It is best known for wintering raptors, sparrows, pipits, and longspurs. 

The most relevant current conservation threat to the San Rafael Valley is mining. As the headwaters of the Santa Cruz River, this area is particularly vulnerable to the water depletion and fouling associated with mining. The Patagonia, Arizona area is presently the location of multiple mining exploration projects.

items.name: Town of Patagonia
items.description: The charming town of Patagonia serves as the start and end point of all the Sky Islands Odyssey routes. Once a supply town for nearby mines and cattle ranches, today, Patagonia is home to multigeneration ranching families, artists, conservationists, retirees, and a flurry of newcomers who are moving to the region specifically for its excellent access to trails and gravel roads. Among many of its varying hats, Patagonia serves as a trail community for Arizona Trail and the launching point for the growing popularity of gravel cycling in the San Rafael Valley. Home to local art galleries, a natural food co-op, a café, a hummingbird sanctuary, a new gathering place for cyclists, and a few places to stay, Patagonia remains a quiet desert hamlet with an eclectic vibe.

items.name: Madera Canyon
items.description: Just slightly off route is Madera Canyon, one of the most famous birding areas in the United States. It is a north-facing valley in the Santa Rita Mountains with riparian woodland along an intermittent stream, bordered by mesquite, juniper-oak woodlands, and pine forests. Madera Canyon is home to over 250 species of birds, including 15 hummingbird species. Visitors from all over the world search for avian specialties such as the Elegant Trogon, Elf Owl, Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher, Red-faced Warbler, and Painted Redstart. A comprehensive bird list published by FoMC is available at the Proctor Visitor Info Station and at trailheads. (https://friendsofmaderacanyon.org/)

items.name: Forest Service Road 143 / Salero Canyon Road
items.description: The surface and difficulty of Forest Road 143/Salero Canyon Road change year-to-year due to monsoons and the way the road is maintained. While the road offers some camping opportunities, incredible views of the Santa Cruz River Valley, and a vast diversity of fauna (a prickly pear cactus next to a cedar tree), this road has a reputation for crushing tired souls who are not mentally prepared for the persistent steep grades and loose surfaces. The rough and tough stuff lasts for approximately 12 miles. Plan accordingly!

items.name: Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory
items.description:
Visible from the route is the Fred Lawrance Whipple Observatory. The Fred Lawrence Whipple Observatory (FLWO) is the largest satellite facility of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory (SAO), part of the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. Located​ on Mt. Hopkins in southern Arizona​, this remote site is home to several telescopes, including the 6.5-meter MMT Observatory. The observatory also includes:
The Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System (VERITAS) gamma-ray observatory.
Telescope arrays designed to find Earth-like exoplanets.
Several other telescopes used for a wide range of astronomical observations.
The observatory is currently closed to the public; however, cyclists can enjoy a long dirt road climb with beautiful views to the 12 KM mark, before turning around.

items.name: Patagonia Mountains
items.description: Following the routes out of the town of Patagonia, cyclists will ride through the Patagonia Mountains, a continuation of the Santa Rita Mountain range divided by Sonoita Creek. The Patagonia Mountains share the same characteristics as the Santa Rita Mountains. The Patagonia Mountains have hundreds of old mine sites. Mining activity began locally in the late 1700s and continued with significant activity from 1857 to the early 1960s. The Patagonia Mountains and Sonoita Creek Watershed are currently threatened by several proposed industrial mining operations that total 39,085 acres (61 square miles) of claims. Learn more at https://www.patagoniaalliance.org/who-we-are/our-ncerns/co

pois.note: The category groups hold waypoints from the bikepacking.com and AZTR GPX files plus the route notes. OpenStreetMap points are a separate group (off by default) and keep their category colour and icon, drawn smaller. Points appear from zoom 9; suggested overnights always. OSM water is unverified: springs and stock tanks in Arizona are seasonal - check the ATA/FarOut AZT Water Report before relying on any of them.

plan.note: Moving time = distance ÷ speed + climb ÷ climbing rate: singletrack 9.5–12 km/h (AZT slowest, Bug Spring Trail 5 km/h), dirt roads 13–15 km/h, pavement 20 km/h; climbing 450 / 550 / 700 m/h. Add breaks on top: December has ~10 h of daylight (Tucson sunrise ~7:15, sunset ~17:25), so days over 7.5 h moving are flagged.
